stories.title: The American Revolution
stories.blurb: How did a quarrel over taxes turn thirteen British colonies into a federal republic with a written constitution?

steps.name: Stamp Act Congress
steps.what: Delegates from nine colonies met in New York and petitioned king and Parliament against the Stamp Act, a tax on printed paper.
steps.why: It was the first joint colonial protest and set out the claim of no taxation without representation; Parliament repealed the act in 1766.

steps.name: Boston Massacre
steps.what: British soldiers fired into a crowd on King Street, killing five men; John Adams later defended the soldiers in court.
steps.why: Patriot printers turned the killings into lasting propaganda against troops stationed in colonial towns.

steps.name: Boston Tea Party
steps.what: Colonists boarded three ships and dumped 342 chests of East India Company tea into the harbour in protest at the Tea Act.
steps.why: Parliament answered with the Coercive Acts, closing Boston's port and pushing the colonies toward united resistance.

steps.name: Battles of Lexington and Concord
steps.what: British regulars sent to seize militia arms at Concord exchanged fire with minutemen and were harried back to Boston.
steps.why: The first shots of the war turned protest into armed rebellion and led to the siege of Boston.

steps.name: Common Sense
steps.what: Thomas Paine published a pamphlet arguing in plain language for independence and against monarchy; it sold tens of thousands of copies within months.
steps.why: It moved public opinion from reconciliation with the king toward a full break.

steps.name: United States Declaration of Independence
steps.what: The Second Continental Congress adopted a declaration, drafted mainly by Thomas Jefferson, that the colonies were free and independent states.
steps.why: It turned a colonial rebellion into a war for a new country and stated its founding principles.

steps.name: Battles of Saratoga
steps.what: After two battles, John Burgoyne surrendered about 6,000 British and German troops to Horatio Gates.
steps.why: The victory convinced France that the Americans could win.

steps.name: Valley Forge
steps.what: About 12,000 Continental soldiers wintered in huts; perhaps 2,000 died of disease, while Steuben drilled the survivors.
steps.why: The army came out of the winter smaller but better trained and more professional.

steps.name: Treaty of Alliance (1778)
steps.what: Benjamin Franklin and fellow commissioners signed a military alliance with France.
steps.why: French money, troops and above all the French navy made the final victory possible.

steps.name: Siege of Yorktown
who: Jean-Baptiste Donatien de Vimeur, comte de Rochambeau
steps.what: American and French forces, with a French fleet blocking the bay, forced Cornwallis to surrender about 8,000 men.
steps.why: The surrender broke Britain's will to continue the land war in America.

steps.name: Treaty of Paris (1783)
steps.what: Britain recognised the independence of the United States, with a western border on the Mississippi.
steps.why: It ended the war and gave the new country a huge territory to govern.

steps.name: Shays's Rebellion
steps.what: Indebted farmers in western Massachusetts closed courts and in January 1787 tried to seize the Springfield armory.
steps.why: The weak national government could do nothing, which persuaded many leaders that the Articles of Confederation had to be replaced.

steps.name: Constitutional Convention (United States)
steps.what: Fifty-five delegates met in secret and wrote a new constitution with a two-house Congress, a president and federal courts.
steps.why: It created the federal system that still governs the United States, including compromises over slavery.

steps.name: First inauguration of George Washington
steps.what: George Washington took the oath as the first president on the balcony of Federal Hall in New York, then the capital.
steps.why: The new constitution began to work as a government.

steps.name: United States Bill of Rights
steps.what: Virginia's ratification completed adoption of the first ten amendments, drafted by James Madison, protecting speech, religion, the press and trial rights.
steps.why: It settled the main objection of opponents of the constitution and closed the founding period.

stories.title: The Haitian Revolution
stories.blurb: How did enslaved people in France's richest colony destroy slavery and found the first Black republic?

steps.name: Saint-Domingue
steps.what: On the eve of revolution about half a million enslaved Africans worked the sugar and coffee plantations of Saint-Domingue, outnumbering whites roughly ten to one.
steps.why: The colony was the most profitable in the Caribbean, and its brutal plantation system was what the revolution overthrew.

steps.name: Ogé's revolt
steps.what: Vincent Ogé, a free man of colour, led a small armed rising demanding equal rights for free people of colour; he was captured and broken on the wheel in February 1791.
steps.why: It showed that the French Revolution's talk of rights had reached the colony, and that the planters would answer with terror.

steps.name: Bois Caïman
steps.what: Enslaved leaders, with Dutty Boukman prominent, met at a night ceremony in the woods to plan a rising.
steps.why: Tradition marks it as the moment the revolution was planned.

steps.name: Haitian Revolution
steps.what: Enslaved people of the Northern Plain rose together, burning hundreds of plantations within weeks.
steps.why: It was the largest slave revolt in the Americas and the start of a thirteen-year war.

steps.name: Sonthonax's emancipation decree
steps.what: French commissioner Léger-Félicité Sonthonax, facing Spanish and British invasion, declared all slaves in the northern province free.
steps.why: Freedom was granted on the ground before Paris approved it, to win Black soldiers to the French side.

steps.name: Law of 4 February 1794
steps.what: The National Convention abolished slavery in all French colonies and made former slaves citizens.
steps.why: It led Toussaint Louverture to leave Spanish service and fight for the French Republic that spring.

steps.name: Toussaint's occupation of Santo Domingo
steps.what: Toussaint Louverture marched east and took over the Spanish part of the island, which Spain had ceded to France in 1795.
steps.why: It put the whole of Hispaniola under his command.

steps.name: Constitution of 1801
steps.what: Toussaint proclaimed a constitution that banned slavery for ever and made him governor for life, while keeping the colony nominally French.
steps.why: Napoleon read it as a bid for independence and decided to retake the colony.

steps.name: Saint-Domingue expedition
steps.what: General Charles Leclerc landed with over 20,000 French troops; Henri Christophe burned Cap-Français rather than hand it over.
steps.why: France aimed to restore control and, as later became clear, slavery.

steps.name: Battle of Crête-à-Pierrot
steps.what: A small garrison held a hill fort against much larger French forces for three weeks before breaking out.
steps.why: Heavy French losses showed that the reconquest would be costly.

steps.name: Death of Toussaint Louverture
steps.what: Seized by trickery in June 1802 and deported, Toussaint died in a cold cell in the Jura mountains.
steps.why: His capture did not end the war; news that France had restored slavery in Guadeloupe drove his former officers back into revolt.

steps.name: Battle of Vertières
who: Donatien-Marie-Joseph de Vimeur, vicomte de Rochambeau
steps.what: Dessalines' army stormed the forts outside Cap-Français; Rochambeau agreed to evacuate the remaining French troops.
steps.why: It was the final defeat of the French army, already ruined by yellow fever.

steps.name: Haitian Declaration of Independence
steps.what: Dessalines proclaimed the independent state of Haiti, taking the island's Taíno name.
steps.why: Haiti became the first state founded by formerly enslaved people and the second independent republic in the Americas.

steps.name: 1804 Haitian massacre
steps.what: On Dessalines' orders, most of the remaining white French population, several thousand people, were killed.
steps.why: It was used abroad for decades to justify isolating the new state.

steps.name: Citadelle Laferrière
steps.what: Work began on a huge mountaintop fortress, built by thousands of labourers and finished under Henri Christophe around 1820.
steps.why: It shows how much the new state feared a French return.

steps.name: Haitian independence debt
steps.what: Under threat from French warships, President Jean-Pierre Boyer accepted a royal ordinance demanding 150 million francs in return for recognition.
steps.why: The indemnity and the loans taken to pay it weighed on Haiti's economy for over a century.

stories.title: Latin American independence
stories.blurb: How did Spain and Portugal lose nearly all of their American empires in less than twenty years?

steps.name: Transfer of the Portuguese court to Brazil
steps.what: Fleeing Napoleon's invasion, the Portuguese royal family and thousands of courtiers sailed to Brazil and set up court in Rio de Janeiro; Brazil's ports were opened to foreign trade.
steps.why: Napoleon's occupation of Iberia left the colonies without a legitimate king in Europe, and in Brazil it put the monarchy itself in America.
steps.wikipedia: Transfer of the Portuguese court to Brazil

steps.name: May Revolution
steps.what: After a week of meetings, a junta replaced the Spanish viceroy of the Río de la Plata.
steps.why: It started self-rule in the south, the base for San Martín's later campaigns.

steps.name: Grito de Dolores
steps.what: The priest Miguel Hidalgo rang his church bell and called his parishioners to revolt; a mass peasant army followed.
steps.why: It began Mexico's war of independence, which was won in 1821.

steps.name: Venezuelan Declaration of Independence
steps.what: A congress in Caracas declared Venezuela independent of Spain, the first Spanish colony to do so formally.
steps.why: The First Republic collapsed within a year, beginning Bolívar's long series of defeats and returns.

steps.name: Jamaica Letter
steps.what: In exile after Spanish reconquest, Bolívar wrote a long letter setting out why Spanish America would and should be free.
steps.why: It is the clearest statement of his political vision, written at his lowest point.

steps.name: Argentine Declaration of Independence
steps.what: The Congress of Tucumán declared the United Provinces of South America independent.
steps.why: It gave San Martín's planned invasion of Chile a declared state behind it.

steps.name: Crossing of the Andes
steps.what: San Martín's route: the Army of the Andes, about 5,000 men, left Mendoza and crossed passes over 3,500 metres high, mainly Los Patos and Uspallata, into Chile.
steps.why: It turned the royalist position in Chile from behind instead of attacking through Upper Peru.

steps.name: Battle of Chacabuco
steps.what: Days after coming down from the mountains, San Martín and O'Higgins defeated the royalists and entered Santiago.
steps.why: Chile became the base for a seaborne attack on Peru, Spain's stronghold.

steps.name: Battle of Boyacá
steps.what: Bolívar's route: from the Venezuelan plains his army crossed the flooded llanos and the Andes by the Páramo de Pisba, then routed the royalists at a bridge near Tunja.
steps.why: Bogotá fell days later, and New Granada gave Bolívar men and money for the rest of the war.

steps.name: Battle of Carabobo
steps.what: Bolívar's army broke the main royalist army in Venezuela.
steps.why: It secured Venezuela's independence inside Bolívar's Gran Colombia.

steps.name: Peruvian War of Independence
steps.what: Having come by sea from Chile, San Martín proclaimed Peru's independence in Lima's main square.
steps.why: The viceroy's army still held the highlands, so the war in Peru was far from over.

steps.name: Battle of Pichincha
steps.what: Antonio José de Sucre defeated the royalists on the slopes of the Pichincha volcano above Quito.
steps.why: It freed what is now Ecuador and brought it into Gran Colombia.

steps.name: Guayaquil Conference
steps.what: The two liberators met privately; no record survives, but soon after San Martín resigned and left Peru.
steps.why: The northern and southern campaigns merged under Bolívar's leadership.

steps.name: Independence of Brazil
steps.what: Prince Pedro, ordered home by Lisbon, declared Brazil independent by the Ipiranga brook and was crowned emperor that December.
steps.why: Brazil became independent as a single monarchy, without breaking into republics as Spanish America did.

steps.name: Battle of Ayacucho
steps.what: Sucre's army defeated and captured the last viceroy of Peru, José de la Serna.
steps.why: It effectively ended Spanish rule on the South American mainland.

steps.name: Congress of Panama
steps.what: At Bolívar's call, delegates from Gran Colombia, Peru, Mexico and Central America met to plan a league of the new states.
steps.why: Its treaties were ratified only by Gran Colombia; the hoped-for union never came.

stories.title: India from Plassey to the Raj
stories.blurb: How did a trading company become the ruler of India, and why did the Crown take over after 1857?

steps.name: Battle of Plassey
steps.what: Robert Clive's small East India Company force beat the Nawab of Bengal after Mir Jafar, his commander, held back his troops.
steps.why: The Company installed Mir Jafar as a puppet and took control of Bengal's wealth.

steps.name: Treaty of Allahabad
steps.what: After victory at Buxar, the Company received from the Mughal emperor the diwani, the right to collect revenue in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa.
steps.why: Land tax, not trade, now paid for the Company and its army.

steps.name: Great Bengal famine of 1770
steps.what: After failed rains, famine killed millions in Bengal, often estimated at about a third of the population, while revenue collection was kept up.
steps.why: It exposed the cost of Company rule for ordinary people and led to the first parliamentary controls on the Company.

steps.name: Permanent Settlement
steps.what: Governor-General Cornwallis fixed Bengal's land tax for ever and made zamindars the owners of the land.
steps.why: It created a landlord class loyal to British rule and left peasants exposed to rising rents.

steps.name: Siege of Seringapatam (1799)
steps.what: British and allied troops stormed Tipu Sultan's capital and Tipu was killed in the fighting, ending the fourth Anglo-Mysore war.
steps.why: The Company's strongest southern rival, who had sought French help, was gone.

steps.name: Battle of Assaye
steps.what: Arthur Wellesley's army of about 9,500 beat a much larger Maratha army of Scindia and Bhonsle.
steps.why: The Marathas, the last great Indian power, began to lose central and northern India to the Company.

steps.date_note: c.; the decline ran from about 1800 to 1840
steps.name: Decline of Dhaka muslin
steps.what: Dhaka's famous fine muslin trade collapsed as cheap machine-made Lancashire cotton flooded India after the Company's trade monopoly ended in 1813, and the city's population fell sharply.
steps.why: India went from exporting cloth to the world to importing British cloth, a key part of its economic subordination.

steps.name: Annexation of the Punjab
steps.what: After the second Anglo-Sikh war, Dalhousie annexed the Sikh kingdom; the boy Maharaja Duleep Singh surrendered the Koh-i-Noor diamond.
steps.why: It completed British control of the subcontinent up to the Afghan frontier.

steps.name: First passenger train in India
steps.what: The first passenger train ran 34 km from Bombay to Thane.
steps.why: Railways bound India's economy to export trade and later moved troops in 1857.

steps.name: Annexation of Awadh
steps.what: The Company deposed Nawab Wajid Ali Shah, citing misrule, and annexed his kingdom.
steps.why: Awadh supplied many Bengal army sepoys, and its annexation fed the anger behind 1857.

steps.name: Indian Rebellion of 1857
steps.what: Sepoys at Meerut, angered by the jailing of comrades who refused new cartridges, killed their officers and rode to Delhi.
steps.why: A mutiny became a wide rebellion across northern India.

steps.name: Siege of Cawnpore
steps.what: Rebels under Nana Saheb besieged the British entrenchment; after the surrender many were killed at the river and the women and children later at the Bibighar.
steps.why: The killings fuelled savage British reprisals across the region.

steps.name: Siege of Delhi (1857)
steps.what: Rebels proclaimed the aged Mughal Bahadur Shah Zafar their emperor; British forces on the Ridge stormed the city in September.
steps.why: The fall of Delhi ended the rebellion's symbolic centre and the Mughal dynasty with it.

steps.name: Siege of Lucknow
steps.what: The British Residency held out for months against rebels, while Begum Hazrat Mahal led resistance in Awadh.
steps.why: Awadh was the heart of the popular rising, not only of the mutiny.

steps.name: Death of Rani Lakshmibai
steps.what: The Rani of Jhansi, whose state had been annexed under the doctrine of lapse, was killed fighting British troops near Gwalior.
steps.why: Her death marked the end of major resistance and made her a lasting nationalist symbol.

steps.name: Government of India Act 1858
steps.what: Parliament transferred the East India Company's powers to the Crown, with a Secretary of State and a Viceroy.
steps.why: Company rule ended and the British Raj began.

stories.title: China's century of humiliation begins
stories.blurb: How did opium, foreign wars and rebellion weaken the Qing empire, and why did its reforms fall short?

steps.name: Destruction of opium at Humen
steps.what: Imperial commissioner Lin Zexu had over 1,000 tonnes of confiscated British opium mixed with lime and salt and washed into the sea.
steps.why: Britain used the seizure as the reason for the First Opium War.

steps.name: British Hong Kong
steps.what: British forces raised the flag and occupied Hong Kong Island during the war.
steps.why: Hong Kong became a British base and free port on China's coast for 156 years.

steps.name: Treaty of Nanking
steps.what: China ceded Hong Kong, opened five ports to British trade and paid 21 million silver dollars.
steps.why: It was the first of the unequal treaties that limited Chinese sovereignty.

steps.name: Jintian Uprising
steps.what: Hong Xiuquan, who believed he was the younger brother of Jesus, proclaimed the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom with an army of followers.
steps.why: It started the Taiping Rebellion, one of the deadliest wars in history.

steps.name: Taiping capture of Nanjing
steps.what: Taiping armies took Nanjing and made it their capital, Tianjing.
steps.why: For eleven years a rival state held the rich lower Yangzi.

steps.name: Yellow River course change
steps.what: Neglected dykes broke and the Yellow River shifted its course hundreds of kilometres north, flooding the plain and reaching the sea north of Shandong.
steps.why: A state absorbed by rebellion could no longer maintain the water works its legitimacy rested on.

steps.name: Burning of the Old Summer Palace
steps.what: In the Second Opium War, Lord Elgin ordered British troops to burn the imperial garden palace after looting it with French forces.
steps.why: The Convention of Peking days later opened more ports and legalised the opium trade.

steps.name: Third Battle of Nanjing
steps.what: Zeng Guofan's Xiang Army stormed Nanjing, weeks after Hong Xiuquan's death.
steps.why: The war, which killed tens of millions, was won by provincial armies, not the old imperial forces.

steps.name: Jiangnan Arsenal
steps.what: Zeng Guofan and Li Hongzhang founded an arsenal in Shanghai to make guns and steamships, with a translation office for Western science.
steps.why: It is the emblem of the Self-Strengthening Movement: Western technology under Confucian rule.

steps.name: Northern Chinese Famine of 1876–1879
steps.what: Drought caused famine across northern China, killing roughly 9 to 13 million people, worst in Shanxi.
steps.why: Relief was slow and poor, showing the limits of the state's reach.

steps.name: Battle of the Yalu River (1894)
steps.what: Japan's navy defeated China's Beiyang Fleet, sinking several ships.
steps.why: China's modern fleet, the pride of Self-Strengthening, lost to a smaller country that had modernised faster.

steps.name: Hundred Days' Reform
steps.what: The Guangxu Emperor issued edicts on schools, exams and the army, advised by Kang Youwei, until Empress Dowager Cixi seized power and confined him.
steps.why: The failure of reform from the top left room for revolution.

steps.name: Siege of the International Legations
steps.what: Boxers and Qing troops besieged the foreign legations for 55 days until an eight-nation army took Beijing.
steps.why: Foreign troops occupied the capital and the court fled to Xi'an.

steps.name: Boxer Protocol
steps.what: China agreed to pay 450 million taels of silver over 39 years and to let foreign troops be stationed in Beijing.
steps.why: The indemnity crippled Qing finances in the dynasty's last decade.

stories.title: Meiji Japan
stories.blurb: How did Japan go from forced opening in 1853 to defeating a European great power in 1905?

steps.name: Perry Expedition
steps.what: Commodore Perry's four American warships anchored off Uraga and delivered a demand that Japan open its ports; he returned in 1854 and got the Convention of Kanagawa.
steps.why: The shogunate's inability to refuse destroyed its prestige.

steps.name: Sakuradamon incident
steps.what: Samurai from Mito killed the chief minister Ii Naosuke, who had signed trade treaties without imperial approval.
steps.why: Political violence against the shogunate grew under the slogan 'revere the emperor, expel the barbarians'.

steps.name: Satchō Alliance
steps.what: Brokered by Sakamoto Ryōma, the rival domains of Satsuma and Chōshū agreed to cooperate against the shogunate.
steps.why: Their combined forces would topple the shogun two years later.

steps.name: Meiji Restoration
steps.what: Satsuma and allied troops seized the palace gates and the court proclaimed the restoration of direct imperial rule under the teenage Emperor Meiji.
steps.why: It ended over 260 years of Tokugawa rule and opened a revolution from above.

steps.name: Battle of Toba–Fushimi
steps.what: Smaller Satsuma and Chōshū forces with modern rifles defeated the shogunate's army south of Kyoto.
steps.why: It opened the Boshin War and the former shogun soon gave up Edo.

steps.name: Battle of Hakodate
steps.what: The last shogunate loyalists under Enomoto Takeaki held out in Hokkaido until they surrendered the star fort of Goryōkaku.
steps.why: The Boshin War ended and the new government ruled all Japan.

steps.name: Abolition of the han system
steps.what: The government abolished the feudal domains and replaced them with prefectures run by officials sent from Tokyo.
steps.why: It created a centralised state and ended the daimyo's power at a stroke.

steps.name: Iwakura Mission
steps.what: About half the government's leaders sailed on a near two-year tour of the United States and Europe to study factories, schools and constitutions.
steps.why: It shaped the leaders' plan to build industry and institutions before seeking equality abroad.

steps.name: Tomioka Silk Mill
steps.what: The state opened a model silk-reeling mill with French machinery, staffed mainly by young women.
steps.why: Silk was Japan's main export and paid for imported machines and warships.

steps.name: Shimbashi–Yokohama railway
steps.what: The emperor opened Japan's first railway, 29 km from Shimbashi to Yokohama, built with British engineers.
steps.why: Rail became a symbol and tool of rapid modernisation.
steps.wikipedia: History of rail transport in Japan

steps.name: Satsuma Rebellion
steps.what: Discontented samurai rose under Saigō Takamori; a conscript army defeated them and Saigō died at Shiroyama.
steps.why: A peasant conscript army beat the samurai, ending the warrior class as a political force.

steps.name: Meiji Constitution
steps.what: The emperor granted a constitution, drafted by Itō Hirobumi on German lines, with an elected lower house.
steps.why: Japan became the first constitutional state in Asia, with power kept close to the throne.

steps.name: Treaty of Shimonoseki
steps.what: After defeating China, Japan gained Taiwan and a large indemnity and China recognised Korean independence.
steps.why: Japan became a colonial power; Russia, Germany and France soon forced it to return the Liaodong peninsula.

steps.name: Anglo-Japanese Alliance
steps.what: Britain and Japan signed a defensive alliance aimed mainly at Russia.
steps.why: It was the first alliance of equals between a European power and an Asian state.

steps.name: Battle of Tsushima
steps.what: Admiral Tōgō's fleet destroyed the Russian Baltic Fleet after its seven-month voyage around the world.
steps.why: Japan won the Russo-Japanese War, the first modern defeat of a European great power by an Asian one.

steps.name: Japan–Korea Treaty of 1910
steps.what: Japan annexed Korea, which it had made a protectorate in 1905.
steps.why: Japan's modernisation ended in an empire of its own; the Emperor Meiji died two years later, in July 1912.

stories.title: The scramble for Africa
stories.blurb: How did European powers carve up almost all of Africa in thirty years, and how did Africans resist?

steps.name: Opening of the Suez Canal
steps.what: The 164 km canal, built by Ferdinand de Lesseps' company largely with Egyptian labour, opened between the Mediterranean and the Red Sea.
steps.why: It made Egypt strategically vital to Britain's route to India; Egypt's debts soon brought foreign control.

steps.name: Kimberley diamond rush
steps.what: Diamond finds drew thousands of diggers to a hill that became the Big Hole, dug by hand; Cecil Rhodes later merged the claims into De Beers.
steps.why: Mineral wealth pulled Britain deeper into southern Africa and built a migrant labour system.

steps.name: Battle of Isandlwana
steps.what: A Zulu army of about 20,000 overran a British camp, killing over 1,300 soldiers.
steps.why: It was one of the worst colonial defeats, though Britain conquered the Zulu kingdom within months.

steps.name: Battle of Tell El Kebir
steps.what: British forces crushed the army of Ahmed Urabi, who had led a nationalist movement against foreign control.
steps.why: Britain occupied Egypt, and other powers rushed to claim territory elsewhere.

steps.name: Berlin Conference
steps.what: Fourteen states met under Bismarck to set rules for claiming African land; no Africans were present. Leopold II's claim to the Congo was recognised.
steps.why: It set the rules for the partition that followed.

steps.name: Siege of Khartoum
steps.what: The Mahdi's forces stormed Khartoum after a ten-month siege and killed General Gordon.
steps.why: A Sudanese Islamic state held off British rule for thirteen years.

steps.name: Witwatersrand Gold Rush
steps.what: Gold found on the Witwatersrand in the Boer South African Republic created Johannesburg almost overnight.
steps.why: The world's largest gold field set British mining interests against the Boer republics.

steps.date_note: the epizootic spread 1887-1897; it reached southern Africa in 1896
steps.name: Rinderpest epizootic
steps.what: A cattle plague brought from Asia swept the continent, killing perhaps 80 to 90 percent of cattle in many regions.
steps.why: Famine and the loss of herds weakened African societies just as conquest came.

steps.name: Battle of Adwa
steps.what: Emperor Menelik II's army, armed with modern rifles, defeated an Italian invasion force of about 17,000.
steps.why: Ethiopia kept its independence, the main exception to the partition.

steps.name: Battle of Omdurman
steps.what: Kitchener's army, with Maxim guns, killed about 12,000 Mahdist soldiers for fewer than 50 of its own dead.
steps.why: Industrial firepower decided the conquest; Sudan came under Anglo-Egyptian rule.

steps.name: Fashoda Incident
steps.what: Kitchener's flotilla met a small French expedition under Marchand that had crossed from the Atlantic; France backed down in November.
steps.why: Britain's Cape-to-Cairo and France's east-west ambitions collided, and the crisis ended in a settlement of spheres.

steps.name: Siege of Ladysmith
steps.what: Boer forces besieged a British garrison for 118 days early in the Second Boer War.
steps.why: The Boer republics' early successes forced Britain to send a far larger army.

steps.name: Second Boer War concentration camps
steps.what: British scorched-earth tactics put Boer families and black Africans in camps, where about 26,000 Boer women and children and at least 14,000 black Africans died; Emily Hobhouse exposed conditions.
steps.why: Britain won the war in 1902, but at a huge civilian cost.

steps.name: Casement Report
steps.what: British consul Roger Casement reported the forced labour, hostage-taking and mutilation used to extract rubber in Leopold II's Congo Free State.
steps.why: International outcry forced Belgium to take the colony from Leopold in 1908.

steps.name: Herero and Nama genocide
steps.what: After the battle of Waterberg, German troops under Lothar von Trotha drove the Herero into the Omaheke desert and later held survivors and the Nama in camps; tens of thousands died.
steps.why: It is widely called the first genocide of the twentieth century.

steps.name: Maji Maji Rebellion
steps.what: Peoples of southern German East Africa, angered by forced cotton growing, rose together, trusting a 'war medicine' water spread by Kinjikitile Ngwale.
steps.why: German scorched-earth repression and famine killed perhaps 75,000 to 300,000 people.

stories.title: The American West and its railroads
stories.blurb: How did the United States take the West from Native nations and Mexico, and what did railroads have to do with it?

steps.name: Louisiana Purchase
steps.what: France formally handed over Louisiana, bought for 15 million dollars, doubling the size of the United States.
steps.why: It gave the young republic claim to the land between the Mississippi and the Rockies, home to many Native nations.

steps.name: Lewis and Clark Expedition
steps.what: The Corps of Discovery set out up the Missouri River to find a route to the Pacific.
steps.why: It mapped the new territory and announced American sovereignty to the nations living there.

steps.name: Fort Mandan
steps.what: The expedition wintered beside the Mandan and Hidatsa villages and hired Toussaint Charbonneau and his Shoshone wife Sacagawea.
steps.why: The expedition depended on Native food, knowledge and guides.

steps.name: Lemhi Pass
steps.what: Lewis crossed the Continental Divide and soon met the Shoshone, led by Sacagawea's brother, who traded horses.
steps.why: There was no easy water route to the Pacific, only mountains.

steps.name: Fort Clatsop
steps.what: The expedition reached the Pacific and spent a wet winter in a log fort near the mouth of the Columbia.
steps.why: It strengthened the American claim to the Oregon Country.

steps.name: Santa Fe Trail
steps.what: After Mexican independence, trader William Becknell took goods from Missouri to Santa Fe, opening a wagon trade route.
steps.why: Commerce drew Americans into Mexico's northern lands long before war.

steps.name: Trail of Tears
steps.what: Under the Indian Removal Act, the army forced about 16,000 Cherokee west to Indian Territory; perhaps 4,000 died.
steps.why: Removal cleared the Southeast for cotton and set the pattern of pushing Native nations west.

steps.name: Oregon Trail
steps.what: About 1,000 settlers in the 'Great Migration' left by wagon for Oregon, a trip of some five months.
steps.why: Hundreds of thousands followed over the next decades, before the railroad replaced the trail.

steps.name: California gold rush
steps.what: James Marshall found gold at Sutter's sawmill; about 300,000 people reached California within a few years.
steps.why: California's native population collapsed under violence and disease, and a rich state grew on the Pacific.

steps.name: Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo
steps.what: Defeated Mexico ceded California and the Southwest, about half its territory, for 15 million dollars.
steps.why: The United States now stretched to the Pacific.

steps.name: Sand Creek massacre
steps.what: Colorado volunteers under John Chivington attacked a peaceful Cheyenne and Arapaho camp, killing about 150 to 200 people, mostly women, children and the old.
steps.why: It hardened war on the Plains for a decade.

steps.name: Golden spike
steps.what: The Union Pacific and Central Pacific lines met, completing the first transcontinental railroad, built in the west largely by Chinese workers.
steps.why: The railroad brought settlers, soldiers and markets onto the Plains.

steps.name: Bison hide trade at Dodge City
steps.what: Dodge City grew on the new Santa Fe railroad as a shipping point for buffalo hides; hunters killed millions of bison in a few years.
steps.why: Destroying the herds destroyed the economic base of the Plains nations.

steps.name: Battle of the Little Bighorn
steps.what: Lakota, Northern Cheyenne and Arapaho warriors killed Custer and about 260 soldiers of the 7th Cavalry.
steps.why: The victory brought a massive army response, and within a year most Lakota were forced onto reservations.

steps.name: Wounded Knee Massacre
steps.what: The 7th Cavalry, disarming Spotted Elk's band of Lakota, opened fire and killed about 250 or more men, women and children.
steps.why: It marked the end of armed Native resistance on the Plains, the same year the census declared the frontier closed.
